title: Trust Is a Behavior, Not a Credential
hook: Credentials tell you who is qualified. They do not tell anyone whether to act on your advice — and acting on advice, at some risk to yourself, is what trust actually is.
key_points: Trust researchers treat trust as a behavior: taking an action that makes you vulnerable because of what someone else told you.
That reframing explains why expertise alone does not produce trust — a credential is evidence of competence, not a reason to accept risk.
The trustworthiness attributes usually cited are benevolence, integrity, openness, and shared values.
Communication settings matter: formal, legalistic venues are built to limit exposure, not to build rapport.
Professor John C. Besley uses the contrast between Aaron Rodgers and Dr. Anthony Fauci to illustrate how frequent, casual engagement can outcompete formal testimony.
His advice to experts is to show motivations and research integrity across many platforms rather than assume credentials do that work.
content_html: Public arguments about expertise usually get framed as a knowledge problem: if only people understood the evidence, they would follow the advice. Trust researchers describe something different. Trust is not an opinion someone holds about you; it is an action they take because of you, one that leaves them worse off if you were wrong.
extra_html: Michigan State communication professor John C. Besley makes that case in The Conversation. If trust is behavior — taking the medication, changing the plan, accepting the recommendation — then the question is not whether an expert is qualified but whether an audience has reason to accept vulnerability. Research on trustworthiness points at four attributes that do that work: benevolence, or evident care for people's wellbeing; integrity, including honesty about the limits of what you know; openness, meaning sharing information and listening; and alignment with an audience's values. Besley illustrates the gap using the contrast between quarterback Aaron Rodgers and Dr. Anthony Fauci, noting that Fauci's most visible appearances were in formal congressional settings structured around legal protection, while Rodgers built familiarity through frequent casual engagement that let audiences see personality and motive. His prescription for experts follows: rather than assume a credential speaks for itself, actively show why the work matters, how it is done, and what values sit behind it, across the platforms where people actually are. The idea generalizes past science communication — it is a useful lens on why official institutions with impeccable qualifications can still fail to be believed.

related.title: Media Trust Is Built Two Ways, Not One
related.hook: Most fixes for distrust in the press ask journalists to try harder. Research on Black communities in Minneapolis found the overlooked half is whether the community engages back.

related.title: Media & Conspiracy Belief
related.hook: Does what you watch shape what you believe? Researchers report that viewing one partisan cable outlet is associated with greater belief in a debunked conspiracy idea.

related.title: How Official Statistics Earn Trust
related.hook: A government statistic carries weight only because of the process behind it. When a report skips the usual methodology and review, the number stops being evidence and becomes an argument.

related.title: Public Opinion & Polling
related.hook: What 'the people' think shapes what governments do — but measuring it is trickier than it looks, and a bad poll can mislead as easily as a good one informs.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean to treat trust as a behavior rather than a feeling?
flashcards.back_html: Trust is measured by whether someone actually acts on your advice in a way that makes them vulnerable — following a recommendation, not merely reporting warm feelings about you.

flashcards.prompt: Which set of attributes does the article identify as driving trustworthiness?

choices.text: Benevolence, integrity, openness, and shared values
Seniority, salary, publication count, and institutional prestige
Speaking volume, camera presence, and follower count alone

flashcards.explanation_html: All four are about character and relationship, which is why credentials alone do not move them.

flashcards.prompt: Why can formal settings work against an expert's trustworthiness?

choices.text: They are designed to limit legal exposure rather than to build rapport or show personality
They legally prohibit experts from explaining their reasoning
Audiences cannot access recordings of formal proceedings

flashcards.explanation_html: Besley contrasts testimony shaped by legal protection with casual, frequent engagement that lets an audience see motivation and character.
